questions.question: Classify economic indicators by timing, giving two correct examples of each class, and explain why unemployment belongs where it does.
questions.expected_answer: Leading indicators change before the economy does — building plans passed, job advertisements, new vehicle sales, factory orders and share prices — and the Reserve Bank's composite leading indicator is watched because it turns months ahead of the cycle. Coincident indicators move with the cycle — industrial production, retail sales and real GDP itself — reporting the economy's current position. Lagging indicators confirm a turning point after it has occurred — unemployment, inventories and insolvencies. Unemployment lags because employers respond to the cycle cautiously in both directions: in a downturn they delay retrenching in the hope conditions improve, and in a recovery they delay hiring until the upswing is confirmed, so jobs move after output. Two further disciplines complete indicator reading: distinguish the level of a variable from its rate of change, since an economy can be large yet shrinking; and distinguish nominal from real values, deflating money figures — nominal GDP growth of 8 percent with 6 percent inflation is real growth of only about 2 percent.

questions.question: Discuss the main social indicators used to judge development, including the two composite measures, and illustrate with South African evidence.
questions.expected_answer: Demographic indicators include population growth and life expectancy at birth, the great summary statistic compressing nutrition, healthcare, sanitation and safety into one number — South Africa's collapsed during the untreated AIDS years and recovered by more than a decade as antiretroviral treatment rolled out. Nutrition and health indicators include the infant mortality rate — deaths before age one per thousand live births, the most sensitive poverty gauge — plus under-five mortality, stunting, HIV prevalence and health-worker ratios. Education indicators cover literacy, enrolment, completion and, critically, learning outcomes, since enrolment without learning flatters the gauge. Service and housing indicators — piped water, sanitation, electricity, formal housing — show post-1994 gains such as electrification reaching about ninety percent of households, while protests mark the remainder. Urbanisation tracks the shift to cities. The composite measures: the UNDP's Human Development Index blends life expectancy, education and income into a score between 0 and 1, dethroning GDP as the sole progress measure; the Gini coefficient measures inequality from 0 to 1, and South Africa's roughly 0,63 to 0,65 is among the highest recorded, making it one of the most unequal societies on earth.

questions.question: Explain the corrections required for honest international comparison of indicators, and distinguish the roles of the IMF and the World Bank in the global economy.
questions.expected_answer: Three corrections: first, compare per capita, since a giant economy like China's can still be far poorer per person than a small rich one. Second, convert at purchasing power parity rather than market exchange rates, because money buys more locally priced goods and services — haircuts, transport, food — in poor countries than raw conversion suggests; PPP can double or triple a developing country's measured income, and honest tables state which basis they use. Third, mind coverage: official statistics miss the informal sector, unpaid household work and subsistence production, all proportionally larger in poorer countries, so measured gaps overstate true gaps; definitions such as unemployment's also differ across countries. The institutions, both created at Bretton Woods in 1944: the IMF conducts surveillance of members' economies and lends short-term to countries in balance-of-payments crises, attaching conditionality — policy changes, often austerity — which makes its rescues both lifelines and lightning rods; the World Bank provides long-term loans and expertise for development projects in infrastructure, education and health, and publishes much comparative data. The clean separation: IMF for short-term crisis finance and stability, World Bank for long-term development. South Africa belongs to both and drew over four billion dollars from the IMF's emergency facility in 2020.
